extracted.intended_audience: farmers, dairy producers, milk handlers, and public-health practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, farm-level guidelines for designing small sewage/septic installations and for preparing, handling, cooling, and selecting milk and meat so as to minimize bacterial contamination and disease transmission. Covers tank sizing and plumbing, underdrain design, stable and utensil hygiene, cooling, and criteria for rejecting diseased meat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Septic tank capacity for single house
rubrics_metrics.description: A tank, in order to do successful work in separating solids and in eliminating as much as possible of the sediment, needs to be of a capacity to equal about one day's flow of the sewage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that many cities build tanks holding only one third or one fourth of daily flow, but for a single house this is not possible; tanks ought to hold at least the full day's flow. Example: Ten persons at 25 gallons each = 250 gallons/day = 33 cubic feet; suitable proportions generally require the tank to be at least 5 times as long as wide; allow extra depth for deposit and scum (an extra foot or more). Example dimensions given: 3 ft wide, 3 ft deep, 5 ft long (≈33 cu ft). Smaller tanks than this are not recommended for a single house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inlet and outlet pipe placement to avoid disturbing scum or sediment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable ... to attach an elbow to the entering pipe so that the sewage enters about halfway between the top and bottom of the tank. Similarly, at the outlet or weir an elbow should be provided because it is not desirable to allow the floating matter of the surface to be carried onto the bed, and a pipe taking off liquid, open halfway between top and bottom, will carry away but little of either the surface scum or bottom sediment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: prevent disturbance of surface scum and bottom sediment and promote uniform distribution across the tank (see Fig.72). This is a recommended detail though almost any kind of tank will answer the purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tank construction materials and dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a tank must be built of concrete or masonry or timber, although the latter is not to be recommended because of its short life. The walls of an ordinary tank may be built 6 inches thick at the top and 12 inches to 18 inches thick at the bottom ... The tank should have 6 inches of concrete on the bottom, and the roof may be made of flagstone or of concrete slabs in which some wire mesh has been buried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timber is discouraged due to short life. Increase wall thickness if depth exceeds 8 feet. Use concrete bottom and robust roof construction with embedded wire mesh for slab strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation and air-space for septic tanks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to ventilate this tank, although it is desirable to have perhaps a foot of air-space between the water level and the roof of the tank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect bad odors during first few months; ventilators will make presence known by odors, but odors often disappear after two or three months as a surface blanket forms. Note rare risk: production of gas in septic tank may be so great that an explosion can occur—be aware of potential hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sizing of dosing/siphon (intermittent discharge) tank
rubrics_metrics.description: The dosing tank must provide for one hour's flow at the maximum rate of flow, and should hold about one fourth of the total daily flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full plant consists of settling tank (raw sewage), a small dosing tank holding ~one hour's flow with automatic siphon for intermittent discharge, and the ground area receiving intermittent discharge completes the installation (see Fig.73). Dosing tank therefore ~1/4 daily flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: When underdrains are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Underdrains will be needed only in cases where the ground water ... comes up so high as to affect the disposal of sewage. Usually no underdrains will be needed unless the ground water gets up to within three feet of the surface, and in clay soils the underdrain is not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underdrains are not for taking care of the sewage directly but for draining off soil-water to prevent interference with soil action on sewage. This principle indicates necessity: install only where groundwater would interfere (within ~3 ft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Underdrain installation specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When used, underdrains should be laid from three to four feet below the surface in parallel lines about fifteen feet apart and on grades of not less than one foot in one hundred. It is always better to have the underdrains too large than too small, and drains less than three inches in diameter should not be used, and they should increase in size to four inches and then to six inches as the separate drains are brought together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No exact rules for size because flow through soils varies: water passes through clay slowly and through gravel rapidly, so larger pipes must be used where soil is coarse. Example observed: six-inch underdrain running full of ground water within 100 feet in gravel soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chemical preservatives in milk; emphasis on sterile handling instead
rubrics_metrics.description: It was at one time common to add to milk certain antiseptics ... The chemicals added were borax, boracic acid, salicilic acid, sodium carbonate, and other similar disinfectants. Gradually, however, it has come to be known that, inasmuch as the milk when first drawn from the cow's udder is sterile ... there is no need of the addition of preservatives, provided particular care is exercised in handling the milk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preservatives may act injuriously on man as well as on bacteria. Prefer preventing bacterial introduction through clean milking, straining, and bottling rather than chemical preservatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two axioms for producing clean milk
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two axioms to be followed if good clean milk is to be produced, and those are that the milking and straining shall be done in clean stables, from clean cows, by clean persons; and the other that the milk shall be cooled to a temperature of fifty degrees or less as soon as received from the cow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two requirements explain why some milk contains millions of bacteria while others have <1000. Enforcing both can reduce bacterial counts dramatically. Both are practical, primary controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable ceiling and hay-handling practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The ceiling of the stable should be entirely dust-tight. Hay should not be taken from the loft or fed to the cows just before milking, because the very moving of a forkful of hay through the air of the stable stirs up so large a number of bacteria ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If loft used, ceiling must be tongue-and-groove and painted so dust doesn’t fall. Best stables have no loft above cattle to avoid dust contamination at milking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light and ventilation in the stable
rubrics_metrics.description: Light and air in a stable are both important ... Ventilation and sunlight are both excellent antiseptics. The ordinary rule ... is four square feet of window surface per cow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value of windows depends on direct sunlight exposure. Provide adequate ventilation and sunlight as antiseptic measures and for cow health; USDA guideline: ~4 sq ft of window per cow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable wall and floor design and cleanliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Walls ... should be absolutely free from dust, and should be smooth, so that they may be brushed or even washed clean. ... Tongue-and-groove sheeting should never be laid horizontally, but rather vertically, and a smooth brick or concrete wall is better than wood in any case. The same care must be taken to have the floor clean and dry. A concrete floor for the stalls and drains is the ideal construction, and both should be thoroughly cleaned morning and night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid horizontal ledges. Keep floors dry and routinely cleaned so no dried refuse remains to host bacteria. Manure should be carried away at least 200 feet to keep barnyard dry, reduce smells, and keep flies away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean the cow before milking
rubrics_metrics.description: The milkman is careful to clean the cow ten or fifteen minutes before the milking is done by sponging or washing her belly, sides, and udder with a damp cloth or with a cloth moistened with a disinfecting solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments: 20,000 bacteria per c.c. when cow rubbed off before milking vs. 170,000 when preliminary cleaning omitted; other example: dirty cows 90,000 per c.c. vs. cleaned cows 2,000 per c.c. Cleaning shortly before milking markedly reduces bacterial load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper milker hygiene and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to squeeze a little milk onto the man's filthy hands and then the handful of milk rubbed around on the cow's teats ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milkers must avoid touching milk with dirty hands; maintain personal cleanliness to prevent transferring bacteria from hands/mouth to milk (can, ladle, strainer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of narrow-topped milk-pail
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the narrow-topped milk-pail ... is of value ... it is startling when tested by bacterial growths under the two conditions to see how many more bacteria will be found in the wide open pail than in the narrow-topped one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pails with small opening (~6 inches diameter) when possible; milker training may be required to use narrow-topped pail effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milk-pail washing and sterilization requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important factor in the care of these utensils is the necessity of killing the bacteria left in them by the milk itself. Ordinary washing will not do this. Either the washing must be done with some sterilizing agent, like strong salsoda, which must then, of course, be thoroughly rinsed out, or else the inside of the pail must be filled with absolutely boiling water or with steam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments: well-washed pails had ~28,600 bacteria per c.c. vs. steamed pails only ~1,300 per c.c. Sterilization by steam or boiling is preferred because rinsing disinfectant risks recontamination by rinse water. Repeated pouring through multiple pails rapidly increases bacteria (example: 6,000→98,000 per c.c. after successive pourings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and care of strainer
rubrics_metrics.description: The strainer for a milk-pail is preferably made of cheesecloth, since this can always be easily boiled between milkings, and so sterilized. A wire strainer ... is in no sense as satisfactory as cheesecloth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strain as soon as each pail is filled; cheesecloth can be boiled/sterilized between uses; wire strainers that require finger manipulation are less satisfactory and increase contamination risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and location of straining and handling of pails
rubrics_metrics.description: The straining should be performed as soon as each pail is filled with milk, and pails of milk should never be allowed to stand around in the barn back of the cows, but rather should be taken at once to the milk-room, where it can be strained before any further contamination takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate removal to a cleaner milk-room for straining reduces airborne and barn-origin contamination. Do not leave pails in barn to collect more contaminants before straining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid cooling of milk to ≤50°F
rubrics_metrics.description: The milk should be cooled, and this, to be effective, must be done in such a way that the temperature of the milk shall at once fall to fifty degrees or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow external cooling (e.g., lowering a can into spring water) cools outer milk slowly and allows bacterial growth internally. Use apparatus that spreads milk in thin sheets over a cooled surface (ice/cold water) to lower temperature rapidly throughout. Example: same milk at room temp went from 4,000 to 270,000 bacteria in 15 hours; kept at 50°F showed no increase for 27 hours and only 12,000 bacteria after 3 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of centralized 'city milk' distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When the milk supplied to the larger cities is furnished as in New York, the impossibility of controlling the quality of the supply becomes apparent ... These are loaded on a train ... reaching the city in the early evening. There it is received and hauled to milk stations ... and the next morning, thirty-six hours old, distributed to the babies of the city as fresh milk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central stations mixing milk from many producers reduce incentive for individual care. Vigorous inspection (e.g., NYC Department of Health) enforcing temperature prescriptions and discarding milk above allowed temperature helps maintain quality. Consumers should be aware of transport age and storage practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milk as a vehicle for infectious diseases (typhoid, diphtheria, scarlet fever, tuberculosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many infectious diseases are propagated by milk ... Four diseases are particularly to be noted in connection with the consumption of milk, namely, typhoid fever, scarlet fever, diphtheria, and tuberculosis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milk may be contaminated by sick persons handling milk (hands, ladles, can covers) or by exudates from nose/throat; mild/unrecognized cases can still transmit. Prevent by excluding sick handlers, strict hygiene, and sanitary practices. Specific historical examples cited (Ithaca typhoid outbreak) illustrate transmission pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using meat from animals showing signs of disease
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing more certain in sanitary science than that the application of heat destroys animal parasites and micro-organisms ... it is here sufficient to say that the flesh of no animal apparently suffering from any disease should be used for food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some diseases are transmissible to humans (trichinosis, tuberculosis, measles of pigs); others spoil flesh and produce toxins (epidemic pneumonia, foot-and-mouth, Texas fever, anthrax, hog cholera). Even when cooking reduces risk, avoid using obviously diseased animals; careful inspection and rejection are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of sick animals prior to slaughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The unhealthy animal can usually be recognized by a casual examination ... characterized by such an examination. When sick, ... the coat ... rough or standing, the nostrils dry or covered with foam, the eyes heavy, the tongue protrudes, the respiration is difficult, movements slow and uncertain ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthy animal: moves freely, bright eye, moist nostril, clear skin, calm respiration, good appetite, chews cud if ruminant. Use these sensory checks to decide on rejection before slaughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: USDA regulations on tuberculous carcasses and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: All carcasses affected with tuberculosis and showing emaciation shall be condemned. All other carcasses affected with tuberculosis shall be condemned, except those in which the lesions are slight, calcified, or encapsulated, and are confined to certain tissues ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: animals only slightly affected with TB with lesions confined to certain organs may be used for food after removing affected parts; carcasses with lesions in more than one or two parts must be rendered at not less than 220°F for four hours into lard or tallow. Use tuberculin test results cautiously; slight lesions may be detected that are not visible to butchers—regulatory rules guide condemnation vs. salvage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting animals for slaughter by general condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The other point to be noted in selecting or rejecting animals for slaughter is their general condition. This means that they should be of the proper weight,—that is, not emaciated, but with a proper amount of fat,—that the flesh should be firm and elastic and the skin supple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer animals well-grown and well-nourished rather than too young or too old. Sensory checks of flesh firmness, elasticity, and skin suppleness indicate suitability for food; avoid emaciated or otherwise improperly conditioned animals.
